Individual Project, DSCI 100 (80 points)¶

INSTRUCTIONS¶

Complete the following questions individually using the provided data set. When prompted, fill out the cells with your code (in code cells) or text (in text cells) to answer the question. The cells will have "%%% EDIT THIS MARKDOWN CELL %%%" or "### EDIT THIS CODE CELL ###" prompting you to overwrite the contents of the cell with your answer.

Your report must be fully reproducible, and run without error by itself with no other files.

REFERENCES¶

Students are required to use methods discussed in DSCI 100 for the project report. However, there may be some stages where you wish to research on how to handle "messy" data, including outliers, missing data, etc. If you refer to anything beyond DSCI 100, please include a link to the reference at the end of this report. It does not need to be a "formal" reference like an academic paper or website, you can link to blog posts or websites like StackExchange if they are relevant to your analysis.

GENERATIVE AI USE¶

This analysis is based on methods learned in DSCI 100, so you should have all of the tools you need to write this code from scratch. Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

I plan to use K-nearest neighbors classification to predict tourney_finish from seed, conf_wins_pct, and reg_wins_pct. KNN is appropriate because the outcome is categorical and the predictors are numeric. It makes no assumptions about the relationship between predictors and outcome.

KNN is sensitive to the scale of the predictors, so I will standardize them first (seed runs 1 to 16 while the percentages run 0 to 100). It struggles with rare categories such as champ and top_2_loss, since few neighbors come from those classes, so the model will likely predict common finishes like first_round_loss more often. It can also be slow on large data sets and is affected by the choice of K.

To process the data, I will first split the tidied data into a training set (70%) and a testing set (30%), using set.seed() for reproducibility and stratifying by tourney_finish so each finish appears in both sets. The split happens before any modelling, so the test set stays untouched. To choose K, I will use 5-fold cross-validation on the training set instead of a separate validation set, and select the K with the highest accuracy. I will standardize the predictors in a recipe so the scaling is learned from the training data only.

I’ll check how well the model does on the test set using accuracy and a confusion matrix. Accuracy shows what share of the predictions the model got right. The confusion matrix shows us which types of errors it makes, which matters here because some finishes have more teams than others. I’ll also compare the accuracy to a baseline that always guesses the most common finish (first_round_loss).

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [18]:
library(tidymodels)

# Keep only the outcome and the three predictors, drop rows with missing values,
# and make sure the outcome is a factor 

model_data <- basketball_tidy |>
  select(tourney_finish, seed, conf_wins_pct, reg_wins_pct) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(tourney_finish = as.factor(tourney_finish))

# Split into training (70%) and test (30%) sets
# strata keeps the mix of finishes similar in both sets

basketball_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.70, strata = tourney_finish)
basketball_train <- training(basketball_split)
basketball_test  <- testing(basketball_split)

# Recipe: tell R what to predict and how to prepare the predictors
# step_scale and step_center put all predictors on the same scale, so seed (1 to 16) doesn't count more than win percentages (0 to 1)

knn_recipe <- recipe(tourney_finish ~ seed + conf_wins_pct + reg_wins_pct,
                     data = basketball_train) |>
  step_scale(all_predictors()) |>
  step_center(all_predictors())


# Model specification, with the number of neighbors left to be tuned

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular",
                             neighbors = tune()) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")


# Choose the best number of neighbors using cross-validation
# We split the training set into 5 folds and try several values of K

knn_vfold <- vfold_cv(basketball_train, v = 5, strata = tourney_finish)

k_values <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 61, by = 4))

knn_results <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(knn_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_spec) |>
  tune_grid(resamples = knn_vfold, grid = k_values) |>
  collect_metrics()

# Keep only accuracy, and plot accuracy for each value of K
accuracies <- knn_results |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy")

ggplot(accuracies, aes(x = neighbors, y = mean)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Cross-Validation Accuracy by Number of Neighbors",
       x = "Number of Neighbors (K)",
       y = "Accuracy estimate")

# Pick the K with the highest accuracy
best_k <- accuracies |>
  arrange(desc(mean)) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(neighbors)
best_k


# Fit the final model on the training set using the best K

final_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular",
                               neighbors = best_k) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |>
  set_mode("classification")

final_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(knn_recipe) |>
  add_model(final_spec) |>
  fit(data = basketball_train)

# Predict on the test set
# Put the real finish and the predicted finish (.pred_class) in one table

predictions <- basketball_test |>
  select(tourney_finish) |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_fit, basketball_test))


# Model accuracy: share of test-set teams predicted correctly

model_accuracy <- predictions |>
  accuracy(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class)
model_accuracy


# Confusion matrix: rows = predicted finish, columns = actual finish
# Shows which types of errors the model makes

predictions |>
  conf_mat(truth = tourney_finish, estimate = .pred_class)
predictions

Task 5.3 Create a Visualization or Table of the Results of your Analysis (4 points)¶

  • Create a visualization or table that is relevant to the results of your analysis (comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow).
  • Describe what this visualization or table is showing, and why it is important to the analysis (approx 150 words or less).

This chart shows what the model predicted for teams at each actual tournament finish in the test set. Each bar is one actual finish, and the colors show how often the model predicted each finish. It is important because accuracy gives only one number, while this shows which types of errors the model makes. The model predicted top_8_loss for teams at every actual finish, including most champs. This is because champs look similar to other strong teams, and most of those teams lost before the final. This shows that K-NN struggles to pick out rare finishes like champ.

In [14]:
# Visualization: what the model predicted for each actual finish
# Each bar is one actual tournament finish (from the test set)
# The colors show what share of those teams the model predicted for each finish
# position = "fill" makes all bars the same length, so we can compare shares

ggplot(predictions, aes(y = tourney_finish, fill = .pred_class)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Predicted Finish for Each Actual Tournament Finish",
       x = "Proportion of Teams",
       y = "Actual Tournament Finish",
       fill = "Predicted Finish")

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

Using seed, conference win percentage, and regular-season win percentage, my K-NN model could predict tournament finish somewhat, but not very well. Cross-validation accuracy was highest at K = 57, and the accuracy on the test set was 0.56. The confusion matrix shows the main weakness: the model predicted top_8_loss for teams at almost every actual finish, including most champs. Rare finishes like champ and top_2_loss were rarely predicted correctly. This means these three variables help a little, but they cannot tell us exactly how far a team will go.

I first tried K values from 1 to 41, and since the best K was near the edge of that range (K=37), I tested larger values to check it, K values from 1 to 61 which gave me the best K value of 57. This was a surprise, because my proposal said the model would mostly predict first_round_loss, but it predicted top_8_loss instead. I did expect rare finishes to be hard to predict, so that part was not surprising. These results show that a team's seed and record are not enough to predict the winner, since single games have a lot of luck in them. For future questions, I could ask whether adding variables known before the tournament, like bid type, first_game_at_home, or conf_rank, improves the predictions. I could also ask whether it is easier to predict a simpler outcome, such as whether a team wins at least one tournament game (using tourney_wins), or whether a different model works better with rare finishes.
